issues.description: The abstract describes the sample as a 'national probability sample' and the Discussion/Strengths section claims 'Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable.' However, the Methods section clearly states participants were 'recruited through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington,' describing a convenience sample of 374 students with a mean age of 19. These descriptions are fundamentally incompatible. A student convenience sample from a single university is not a national probability sample. This contradiction undermines the entire framing of the study's contribution (which is predicated on extending prior student-sample findings to a general population).
issues.quote: We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington.

issues.subcategory: Confidence intervals inconsistent with reported N
issues.description: The confidence intervals in Table 1 are far too narrow for N=374. For example, the SDO mean of 2.60 (SD = 0.96) with N=374 would yield a 95% CI of approximately [2.50, 2.70], yet the reported CI is [2.58, 2.63]. Similarly, the correlation between SDO and environmentalism (r = -.25) with N=374 should yield a 95% CI of approximately [-.35, -.15], but the reported CI is [-.27, -.22]. The reported CIs are consistent with a sample size of several thousand, not 374. This suggests either the data are from a different (much larger) sample than described in the methods, or the confidence intervals are miscalculated.

issues.subcategory: Degrees of freedom inconsistent with described model
issues.description: The reported model has df = 2279, which is far too large for a path analysis with 3 observed composite variables across 5 time points (which would yield approximately 120 unique variance/covariance elements). A df of 2279 is consistent with item-level analysis involving ~70 observed variables, but the text describes path analysis at the construct level. Either the analysis is not as described, or the df is incorrect. This makes it impossible to evaluate the appropriateness of the model.

The chi-square difference test comparing the bidirectional SDO-RWA cross-lagged paths is reported as χ2(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001. A chi-square difference of over 15,000 with 1 degree of freedom is implausibly large for any realistic sample size, and would be essentially impossible with N=374. This value is almost certainly an error (possibly a data entry or formatting error), and it calls into question the validity of all chi-square difference tests reported in the results.

The environmentalism measure is described in the Methods as two items assessing environmental concern ('How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?' and 'To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?'). However, throughout the Results and Discussion, the outcome variable is referred to as 'willingness to sacrifice for the environment' or 'willingness to make sacrifices for the environment.' Environmental concern and willingness to sacrifice are distinct constructs (the attitude-behavior gap is well-documented in environmental psychology). The items described do not measure willingness to change behavior, which is what the abstract and title claim the study examines.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as participants' concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley's [28] environmental concern scale

issues.description: The Data Analysis section states 'We present standardized parameters,' but Figure 1 is described as presenting 'Unstandardized parameters,' and the results section reports coefficients as 'B' (the conventional notation for unstandardized coefficients). These are contradictory. It is unclear which type of parameters was actually reported, making interpretation of effect sizes impossible.
issues.quote: We present standardized parameters, which vary across time points due to differences in observed variances.

issues.subcategory: Standard error reported as standard deviation
issues.description: Throughout the Results section, the uncertainty around path coefficients is reported as 'SD' (standard deviation). In path analysis/SEM, the appropriate measure of uncertainty for parameter estimates is the standard error (SE), not the standard deviation. Reporting SD instead of SE is either a labeling error or reflects a fundamental misunderstanding of the output. If the values are truly SDs rather than SEs, they would be incorrect for inference.
issues.quote: SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice (B = -.11, SD = .01, p < .001, 95% CI [-.13, -.09]) than RWA (B = -.02, SD = .01, p = .001, 95% CI [-.05, -.01]).

issues.subcategory: Non-significant difference interpreted as supporting differential prediction
issues.description: The chi-square difference test comparing SDO and RWA as predictors of environmentalism was non-significant (χ2(1) = 2.34, p = .126), meaning the constrained model (equal paths) fit comparably to the unconstrained model. Despite this, the authors interpret SDO as 'a stronger predictor' based on 'the pattern of unstandardized coefficients.' This contradicts their own statistical test, which failed to find a significant difference. The entire framing of the paper depends on SDO being the stronger predictor, yet their formal test does not support this claim.
issues.quote: We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data χ2(1) = 2.34, p = .126, but based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor

issues.subcategory: Inappropriate causal claims from cross-lagged panel model
issues.description: The Discussion makes explicit causal claims: 'These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism' and 'this strengthens our confidence in SDO having a causal effect on environmental attitudes.' Cross-lagged panel models (CLPMs) cannot establish causality. They show temporal precedence but confound between-person and within-person variation (as shown by Hamaker et al., 2015). The observed cross-lagged effects may reflect stable between-person differences rather than within-person causal processes. The authors do not acknowledge these well-known limitations of CLPMs.
issues.quote: These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism.

issues.description: The Data Analysis section states 'we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings.' However, Figure 1's note states 'All meet our accepted threshold for significance of p < .01 unless otherwise noted.' These are different thresholds applied within the same study without explanation.
issues.quote: we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings

issues.subcategory: Missing attrition information and inappropriate handling
issues.description: With five waves of data collection over five years, attrition is likely substantial. No information about attrition rates, dropout patterns, or whether dropout is related to the study variables is provided. The use of listwise deletion (stated in the Methods) is inappropriate for longitudinal data, as it discards all data from participants who missed any wave, reduces power, and can introduce bias if data are not missing completely at random (MCAR). Full information maximum likelihood (FIML) or multiple imputation would be more appropriate. The number of participants with complete data across all 5 waves is not reported.
issues.quote: Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion.

issues.subcategory: False claim of nationally representative sample
issues.description: The Strengths and Limitations section claims 'Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population.' However, the described sample (374 introductory psychology students, mean age 19, 68% female, 86% NZ European) is neither nationally representative nor generalizable to the NZ population. This claim directly contradicts the methods section and substantially overstates the external validity of the findings.
issues.quote: Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population.

issues.description: One RWA item was not assessed at Time 2 but was included at all other time points, meaning the RWA construct is measured with 5 items at T2 and 6 items at all other time points. This introduces measurement non-invariance across time, potentially confounding substantive change with measurement change. No measurement invariance testing is reported, and no discussion of how this inconsistency was handled (e.g., whether the item was excluded at all time points, or whether different composites were used).
issues.quote: The item "Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the "normal way" things are supposed to be done", was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points.

issues.description: Reliability estimates are reported for SDO (.69) and RWA (.70) in Table 1, but the environmentalism measure consists of only 2 items and its reliability is reported as .76. While a 2-item scale can be evaluated via inter-item correlation, this should be explicitly discussed given the serious measurement limitations of using only 2 items to capture a complex construct like environmentalism. Furthermore, reliability at later time points is not reported for any measure.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as participants' concern about environmental problems.

issues.description: The Data Analysis section states the same constraint twice: 'We started by constraining the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point' and then 'Finally, we constrained the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point.' This appears to be a copy-paste error and raises the question of whether a different constraint was intended to be described in one of these sentences.
issues.quote: We started by constraining the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point... Finally, we constrained the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point.

issues.subcategory: Poor model fit dismissed without justification
issues.description: The CFI of .86 falls below both the conventional cutoff of .90 and the more stringent .95 recommended by Hu and Bentler (1999). The authors dismiss this by attributing it to 'model complexity,' but do not provide evidence or citations supporting this interpretation. Selectively accepting fit indices that favor the model while dismissing those that do not is problematic. Furthermore, the chi-square value of 36,511.73 is enormous even given the df, suggesting substantial misfit.
issues.quote: model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03, 90% CI [.025, .026], SRMR = .07)

issues.description: The authors state 'Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05.' This logic is inverted: with large sample sizes, researchers typically adopt more stringent thresholds because trivially small effects become statistically significant. Furthermore, N=374 is not particularly large for a cross-lagged model with 3 variables across 5 time points. If the actual sample is much larger (as CIs suggest), the justification becomes even more inappropriate.
issues.quote: Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings.

issues.description: The authors use a traditional cross-lagged panel model (CLPM) without acknowledging its well-documented limitations. Hamaker, Kuiper, and Grasman (2015) demonstrated that CLPMs confound between-person and within-person effects, and can produce misleading results. A random intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) would be more appropriate for separating stable trait-like differences from within-person change processes. Without this, the cross-lagged effects may simply reflect between-person confounds rather than within-person temporal influence.

issues.subcategory: Missing descriptive statistics for later time points
issues.description: Only Time 1 descriptive statistics are provided in Table 1. For a five-wave longitudinal study, means, SDs, reliabilities, and correlations at all time points (and cross-time correlations) are essential for evaluating the data, understanding patterns of change, and enabling replication.
issues.quote: Table 1. Descriptive statistics at Time 1.

issues.description: The Results section states that 'SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice were all relatively stable over time' but does not report the actual autoregressive path coefficients or their significance levels. These are essential for evaluating the stability claim and interpreting the cross-lagged effects.
issues.quote: SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice were all relatively stable over time, consistent with our prediction that these variables remain largely unchanged over the study period.

issues.subcategory: No pre-registration or alternative model comparisons
issues.description: There is no mention of pre-registration. Multiple analytic decisions (stationarity constraints, which fit indices to prioritize, how to handle the missing RWA item, listwise deletion) represent researcher degrees of freedom. No alternative models (e.g., unconstrained model, model without stationarity assumption) are compared to assess the sensitivity of findings to these choices. The authors also do not justify why the stationary model was chosen beyond stating they were 'more interested in the overall and comparative effects.'
issues.quote: We imposed this stationary cross-lagged model because we were more interested in the overall and comparative effects of SDO and RWA on changes in environmentalism

issues.subcategory: Student sample contradicts paper's stated contribution
issues.description: The paper's entire rationale is that previous longitudinal research used student samples and found different patterns than cross-sectional general population studies. The stated contribution is examining this relationship in a 'general population sample.' However, if the actual sample is psychology students (as the Methods state), the paper does not deliver on its core contribution, and findings would be expected to replicate Stanley et al. (2017) rather than extend them.
issues.quote: The present paper advances this research by examining the impact of SDO and RWA on environment-related attitudes in a general population sample, spanning five years.

issues.subcategory: Contradictory findings relative to stated predictions
issues.description: The authors predict that in a general population sample, SDO will be a stronger predictor than RWA (based on meta-analytic findings). However, their formal statistical test shows no significant difference between SDO and RWA as predictors (p = .126). Yet the Discussion treats the SDO > RWA finding as confirmed, stating it is 'consistent with our predictions.' If the sample is actually a student sample, the predictions and interpretation would need to be entirely reconsidered.
issues.quote: Our main finding was consistent with our predictions and the majority of cross-sectional research: Across five years, SDO was the strongest ideological predictor of environmentalism.

issues.description: The RMSEA 90% CI is reported as [.025, .026], which is an implausibly narrow range (only .001 wide). RMSEA confidence intervals are typically much wider. This may reflect a reporting error in the lower and/or upper bound.

issues.subcategory: Missing information on effective sample size
issues.description: Given the use of listwise deletion across five waves, the effective sample size for the analyses could be substantially smaller than the reported N of 374. The actual number of participants with complete data on all variables at all time points is not reported, making it impossible to assess statistical power or the degree of data loss.
issues.quote: Of the 374 participants included in this study

issues.description: For meaningful comparisons of constructs across time in longitudinal research, measurement invariance should be established. This is particularly important given that the RWA scale changes between time points and that short measures with marginal reliabilities are used. No measurement invariance testing is reported or discussed.

Cross-lagged path coefficients are small (B = -.11 and B = -.02 for SDO and RWA respectively, or B = -.04 and -.01 for the reverse paths). Without standardized coefficients clearly reported (given the standardized/unstandardized confusion), it is impossible to evaluate the practical significance of these effects. No discussion of effect sizes or their practical meaning is provided.

The methods describe data collected 'across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013).' Five semesters spanning five calendar years (2009-2013) implies roughly one semester per year, but the phrasing suggests academic semesters, which would typically cover only 2.5 years. This inconsistency raises questions about the actual timing of measurements and the length of the inter-wave intervals.
issues.quote: This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013).
